t.3.22.1: As that dreadful army set out, a great, thundering cloud, dusky red like a donkey, rained down upon it an inauspicious shower of blood in place of water.
t.3.22.2: His swift horses, yoked to the chariot, suddenly fell down of their own accord on a level, flower-strewn spot of the royal road.
t.3.22.3: A dark halo with a blood-red rim appeared, encircling the sun, which looked like a whirling firebrand.
t.3.22.4: Then a huge and most dreadful vulture approached the lofty banner with its golden staff, alighted upon it, and stayed there.
t.3.22.5: And near Janasthāna, flesh-eating beasts and birds with harsh voices, having gathered together, raised cries of many discordant kinds.
t.3.22.6: And in the blazing quarter of the sky, dreadful jackals with mighty voices uttered a terrifying cry, ill-omened for the Yātudhānas.
t.3.22.8: A dreadful, hair-raising darkness arose, and neither the cardinal directions nor the intermediate quarters could be clearly seen.
t.3.22.7: Fearsome clouds, like shattered mountains and bearing parched waters, made that sky no sky at all.
t.3.22.10: Jackals of dreadful aspect, ever bringers of ill fortune in battle, howled facing the army, with mouths spewing flames.
t.3.22.9: Though it was not the hour of twilight, it glowed with the colour of fresh, wet blood. Then fearsome beasts and birds cried out, facing Khara.
t.3.22.11: A headless trunk, looking like an iron club, was seen near the sun, and the great planet Svarbhānu seized the sun out of season, when it was no time for an eclipse.
t.3.22.12: The wind blew swiftly, the sun became lustreless, and even without night the stars rose up, gleaming like fireflies.
t.3.22.13: At that moment the lotus pools, with their flowering lotuses, saw their fish and birds shrink away into hiding, and the trees became bare of flowers and fruits.
t.3.22.14: There the mynah birds kept screeching, crying out “vīcī-kūcī.”
t.3.22.15: Meteors of terrifying aspect fell with a thunderous roar, and the earth too trembled, together with its mountains, woods and forests.
t.3.22.16: As the wise Khara stood in his chariot, roaring, his left arm trembled, and his harsh cry stuck in his throat.
t.3.22.17: As he looked about on every side, his vision grew filled with tears, and a pain arose in his forehead; yet, out of delusion, he did not turn back.
t.3.22.18: Having observed those great portents that had arisen, making the hair stand on end, Khara, laughing, then spoke to all the rākṣasas.
t.3.22.19: Through my valour I pay no heed to all these great portents that have arisen, terrible to behold, just as a strong man pays no heed to weaklings.
t.3.22.20: With my sharp arrows I could bring down even the stars from the vault of the sky; enraged, I would yoke Death himself to the law of dying.
t.3.22.21: Without slaying with sharp arrows that Rāghava, puffed up with his strength, and his brother Lakṣmaṇa as well, I cannot bring myself to turn back.
t.3.22.22: May my sister have her desire fulfilled once she has drunk the blood of those two, she for whose sake this downfall of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa comes about.
t.3.22.23: Never before in battles have I met with defeat anywhere; this is evident to you yourselves, and I do not speak a falsehood.
t.3.22.24: Enraged, I could slay in battle even the king of the gods, thunderbolt in hand, riding upon the rutting Airāvata; how much more, then, those two humans!
t.3.22.25: Hearing the roar of that rākṣasa, that great army, already bound by the noose of death, attained unequalled delight.
t.3.22.26: And the great-souled ṛṣis, the devas and gandharvas, and the siddhas together with the cāraṇas assembled there, eager to witness the battle.
t.3.22.28: May Rāghava conquer in battle the night-roaming descendants of Pulastya, just as the one with the discus in hand conquered in battle all the foremost of the Asuras.
t.3.22.27: Having come together, those beings of meritorious deeds spoke to one another: “May there be well-being for cows and brāhmaṇas, and for those who are esteemed in the worlds.”
t.3.22.29: Speaking this and much else again and again, the great seers beheld the army of those rākṣasas whose lives were spent.
t.3.22.30: Khara, in his chariot, swiftly rushed out from the front of the army; and seeing that rākṣasa, the rākṣasas too rushed forth once more.
t.3.22.32: Meghamālī, Mahāmālī, Sarpāsya and Rudhirāśana: these twelve of great valour set out, surrounding Khara on every side.
t.3.22.31: Śyenagāmī, Pṛthugrīva, Yajñaśatru, Vihaṃgama, Durjaya, Karavīrākṣa, Paruṣa and Kālakārmuka were among them.
t.3.22.33: Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, Pramāthī, and likewise Triśiras, these four foremost of the army, followed close behind Dūṣaṇa.
t.3.22.34: That army of heroic rākṣasas, terrible in its onset, eager for battle and exceedingly dreadful, swiftly fell upon the two princes, like a garland of planets closing upon the moon and the sun.
